title: Detection Strategy for Phishing across platforms.
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Phishing across platforms.
summary: This strategy detects phishing as a delivery plus effect pattern rather than as a spam classification problem, covering malicious attachments, malicious links, links to services that host the payload, and voice or callback lures that lead to a message. Phishing matters because it converts human judgement into initial access, and it is the entry step for a large share of intrusions, so detection here buys response time before the intruder gains a foothold. Useful telemetry includes mail flow records with sender, recipient, attachment type and URL, browser and mail client process creation on the endpoint, proxy and DNS records for the clicked link, and mailbox rule changes that follow a successful compromise. The main failure is volume and framing: mail security already filters most attempts, and analysts drown in low confidence reports, so the strongest rules correlate a delivered message with real endpoint activity on the same user and host.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for harmful email that reaches a person, and for what happens on the computer afterward. Harmful email often carries a bad file or a link to one. It can also invite the reader to call a phone number. The detection joins the message with the activity that follows it.
beginner.whyItMatters: A message that gets through uses a person as the way in. Technical controls rarely stop that step on their own. Reports from users also arrive slowly, so machine signals are faster. Linking the message to the click shows which reports are real. That lets your team focus on the users who actually opened something.
howItWorks: The mail system records each delivered message, its sender, its links and any attachment.
The endpoint records browser and mail client processes, plus any file that arrives.
Proxy and name lookup records, called DNS logs, show which links were actually opened.
The mailbox audit log shows new forwarding rules or inbox changes.
A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management system) joins all of these by user and time.
A delivered message followed by a click and a download or rule change raises the alert.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk that writes down every guest who arrives. The book alone proves nothing. One guest checks in, takes the service lift to the manager's office and changes the locks. That guest is worth a phone call.
takeaways: Treat phishing as a chain from delivery to effect, not as a spam score.
The click and the download are what confirm a report is worth chasing.
A new mail forwarding rule after a message often means the account is already lost.

objectives: Describe the phishing variants covered and how each reaches the user.
Identify the mail, endpoint, proxy and mailbox audit fields needed to prove the chain.
Correlate a delivered message with endpoint and network activity for the same user and host.
Recognise mailbox rule creation and forwarding changes as post compromise indicators.
Tune the rule so that awareness training and bulk mail do not dominate the alert queue.
dataSources: Email gateway or mail platform message trace records with sender, recipient, subject, attachment names and extracted URLs
Mailbox audit log entries for new inbox rules, forwarding configuration changes and sign in events from new locations
Sysmon event 1 process creation showing a mail client or browser spawning a child process or script interpreter
Web proxy logs with the click time, client address, requested URL and response content type
DNS resolver logs showing lookups for domains that appear in delivered message bodies
logic: The rule treats a delivered message with a suspicious characteristic as a candidate rather than an alert, then requires corroborating activity from the same user or host within a short window. Inputs are the message trace record with sender domain, authentication results, attachment type and URL, the mailbox audit entry for rule changes or unusual sign ins, and endpoint or network events showing a click, a download or a spawned process. The fields to join are the recipient address or mailbox identifier, the sending domain and URL, the host name, and the timestamps of delivery and of the endpoint action. The benign case is bulk business mail, newsletter traffic and user reported messages that never produce any endpoint effect, or an internal sender whose domain passes authentication and who sends to a known distribution list. The malicious case is a message that fails sender authentication or uses a lookalike domain, carries an archive, script or shortcut attachment or a link to a newly registered host, and is followed by a browser process handing off to a script interpreter, a credential prompt page, or a new mail forwarding rule created minutes later.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Delivered Mail With Suspicious Attachment Followed by Endpoint Execution
# logsource:
#   product: email
#   category: mail_gateway
# detection:
#   selection_mail:
#     AttachmentExtension|contains:
#       - '.zip'
#       - '.htm'
#       - '.lnk'
#       - '.iso'
#   selection_auth:
#     SpfResult: 'fail'
#     DmarcResult: 'fail'
#   filter_training:
#     SenderDomain|endswith: 'awareness-training.example'
#     Subject|contains: 'security awareness'
#   condition: selection_mail and selection_auth and not filter_training
# level: medium
falsePositives: Legitimate bulk mail from a marketing platform that has not yet configured sender authentication records for its sending domain
Suppliers and partners who send invoices or shipping documents as archive attachments from a domain with misconfigured mail records
Internal departments using a mass mailing tool that relays through a third party service and fails the alignment check
Security awareness training campaigns that simulate phishing and therefore look identical to a real attempt until the sender is checked
tuningNotes: Start with the endpoint confirmation half of the rule, alerting only when a delivered message leads to a process or download on the recipient host, which keeps volume low and findings actionable, then add mail only signals as a lower severity queue for triage. Filter the awareness training sender and your own bulk mailing platforms explicitly, and maintain a list of partner domains so their authentication failures do not generate repeat alerts. The coverage you lose is a phishing message that produces no immediate endpoint effect, for example a credential harvesting page that never downloads anything, so pair this rule with alerts on success sign ins from new user agent strings or unusual locations after a delivered message.
